directions.hypothesis: The Fitness Browser genes important in the tryptophan-related conditions are mainly biosynthetic and regulatory rather than catabolic. Spent medium from the producing strain restores growth of tryptophan auxotrophs from the same groundwater community.
directions.outcomes: Support: biosynthetic genes dominate the list, and spent medium supports auxotroph growth at a level matching added tryptophan. Refute: catabolic or transport genes dominate the list, or spent medium gives no growth beyond the non-producer control, so the released tryptophan is not available to neighbours at useful levels.
directions.prior_work: PMID 30208844 and PMID 35694313 describe the exometabolomics resource and soil-bacteria medium. PMID 37322284 and PMID 35592760 study auxotroph provisioning in engineered or cultured consortia. None asks whether a natural groundwater strain's released tryptophan sustains auxotrophs while the same strains fail to grow on it.
directions.question: Tryptophan rose in the Web of Microbes exometabolome of a groundwater Pseudomonas fluorescens, yet 0 of 50 strains used it as a carbon source. Is the released tryptophan biosynthetic overflow that neighbours can use, or a by-product with no ecological role?
directions.readiness_basis: The gene lists and pathway calls are in the lakehouse, but no spent-medium or auxotroph growth measurements exist.
directions.test: Step 1, lakehouse: split the 231 tryptophan-associated Fitness Browser genes of the FW300 strains by pathway role (biosynthesis, catabolism, regulation, other) using pathway-step calls from the Pangenome Collection, and by whether tryptophan was a carbon source, a nitrogen source or only present in rich medium. Step 2, experiment: grow the producer, collect spent medium, and test growth of tryptophan auxotrophs. Candidates are Oak Ridge isolates whose pathway call lacks a complete tryptophan route, or a tryptophan-deletion mutant in a reference strain. Controls are fresh medium with and without added tryptophan, and spent medium from a non-producing strain.
directions.title: Is tryptophan released by Pseudomonas fluorescens overflow metabolism that cross-feeds auxotrophs?
directions.why_it_matters: It would show that a metabolite being produced, having fitness genes and having a complete pathway does not imply it is eaten. It would also name a concrete cross-feeding route in groundwater communities, and a rule for reading exometabolite data.

directions.hypothesis: Within fitness modules, members that are adjacent on the chromosome are co-inherited across genomes far more than non-adjacent members, and non-adjacent members show no more co-inheritance than matched random gene sets. This explains why pairwise and module signals look weak when pooled.
directions.outcomes: Support: adjacent pairs are co-inherited well above matched random sets, while non-adjacent pairs are not. Refute: non-adjacent module members are also co-inherited above matched random sets, which would mean the weak pooled signal is not explained by adjacency, or neither class exceeds the random sets.
directions.prior_work: PMID 38948139 links cofitness network connectivity to essentiality in open pangenomes and PMID 38323821 derives functional modules from fitness data in Pseudomonas putida. Neither asks whether co-inheritance of module members depends on chromosomal adjacency.
directions.question: Pairs of genes with similar fitness profiles are only weakly linked to co-occurrence across genomes, and module-level field activity was unrelated to conservation in Desulfovibrio vulgaris Hildenborough. Is shared inheritance of functionally coupled genes confined to physically adjacent genes, such as operons and islands?
directions.readiness_basis: Module membership, gene order and genome presence tables are in the lakehouse, but the matched-random comparison across species must be built.
directions.test: For organisms in the Fitness Browser that have fitness modules, take auxiliary genes only, at below 95% prevalence. Use the Pangenome Collection to compute co-occurrence of module members across genomes of the same species. Split member pairs into adjacent (within a few genes) and non-adjacent. Compare each class with random auxiliary gene sets matched on prevalence and on mean fitness, including the Desulfovibrio vulgaris Hildenborough modules from the field-versus-lab analysis.
directions.title: Are cofitness modules co-inherited across genomes only when their genes sit next to each other?
directions.why_it_matters: It would explain the disagreement between projects on whether modules rescue weak fitness-to-genome links. It would also tell analysts to define units by genomic adjacency rather than by fitness similarity alone when inferring selection from co-occurrence.

directions.hypothesis: Condition classes served by a few dedicated, widely shared genes (biosynthesis of amino acids and nucleosides) are predictable from gene content. Classes that depend on many diffuse, lineage-specific genes (metals, antibiotics) are not. The predictive gene groups are combinations of variable-prevalence genes that stand in for genus, so any link to fitness genes is expected to be partial.
directions.outcomes: Support: classes with few, conserved fitness genes are predictable and classes with many, accessory fitness genes are not, across classes and across organisms, with the relation surviving within genera. Refute: predictability is unrelated to gene number and conservation, or the relation disappears within genera, which would point to lineage structure or measurement noise rather than gene requirements.
directions.prior_work: PMID 29769716 and PMID 25968644 provide genome-wide mutant fitness across diverse bacteria, and PMID 36097170 shows essentiality is strain-dependent in a bacterial pan-genome. None asks why some condition classes are predictable from gene content and others are not.
directions.question: Gene content predicted growth for amino acids, tryptophan, nucleosides and carbon sources, but not for metals, antibiotics or nitrogen sources. Is predictability set by how many genes, and how conserved, a condition requires, given that the predictive gene groups act as genus-level proxies rather than individually established causal genes?
directions.readiness_basis: Fitness data, pangenome conservation and the growth panel are in the lakehouse, but the per-class gene counts and within-genus comparisons must be computed and aligned across organisms.
directions.test: For the Oak Ridge isolate growth panel in ENIGMA CORAL and the 343 tested conditions, use Fitness Browser data for the organisms the model work names (for example Cupriavidus Cup4G11 and Pseudomonas N1B4). For each condition class count genes with strong fitness effects and the share of them that are core in the Pangenome Collection. Test whether these two numbers explain which classes were predictable, including the 95 conditions that were. Treat the predictive gene groups as genus-level proxies: for each class also measure how much the predictive groups overlap the fitness genes, noting that this overlap ranged from 1.72 times chance in Cup4G11 to 0.83 times in N1B4, and check whether class predictability still tracks gene number when the comparison is restricted to within-genus variation. Order the classes before looking at prediction results.
directions.title: Does growth predictability from gene content track how many genes a condition class needs?
directions.why_it_matters: It would explain which phenotypes can be read from genomes and which need direct measurement. It would also tell experimenters where genome-based prediction can replace growth assays, while showing how far the predictive gene groups reflect mechanism rather than lineage.

directions.hypothesis: Within species whose whole-genome gene content shows no environment link, accessory genes in defense and mobile-element categories still track isolation environment after phylogeny is removed, while housekeeping categories do not.
directions.outcomes: Support: some categories, most likely defense and mobile elements, stand out against the shuffled null in species with no whole-genome environment effect. Refutation: no category beats the null, so the weak environment signal is genuinely weak or limited by the metadata.
directions.prior_work: PMIDs 29975997 and 33602135 report weak habitat signal within single species; this tests, across many species at once, whether the signal sits in particular functional categories that a whole-genome measure averages away.
directions.question: Whole-genome gene content barely tracks environment in most species. Does environment instead select particular functional gene categories, such as defense or mobile elements, within species?
directions.readiness_basis: Gene-cluster presence/absence and isolation-source labels already exist for the species analysed in the ecotype work.
directions.test: Take the species in the Pangenome Collection with enough genomes and direct isolation-source labels. Per species, test each accessory gene family and each functional category for association with environment, holding phylogenetic distance fixed. Compare the observed category-level association with a null built by shuffling environment labels among close relatives. Run this for the species, most of those analysed, in which the whole-genome environment effect was absent.
directions.title: Is environmental adaptation hidden in a few gene categories rather than whole genomes?
directions.why_it_matters: It would show that the widespread 'environment does not matter' result comes from averaging over all genes. Ecotype studies would then need to be built around specific functions, not whole-genome similarity.

directions.hypothesis: In host-associated species, gene content varies with body site or tissue of isolation more strongly than with geographic or satellite-embedding distance, while in free-living species the reverse holds.
directions.outcomes: Support: body site explains more than embedding distance in host-associated species and not in free-living species. Refutation: body site adds nothing beyond embeddings, or the lifestyle contrast stays absent.
directions.prior_work: PMIDs 31227022, 34523223, 32503908 and 36445161 used direct environmental measurements in host systems; this tests whether host microenvironment, not collection coordinates, explains the missing lifestyle contrast in genome-scale data.
directions.question: Why do host-associated and free-living bacteria look equally weak in environment-gene-content links, when published work finds host-associated communities less responsive to the environment? Is collection-site location the wrong variable for hosts?
directions.readiness_basis: Source text exists but body-site harmonisation and per-species distance models must be built.
directions.test: Select species in the Pangenome Collection that have many genomes from both host and non-host sources, including the clinical-heavy species. Harmonise body site or tissue from isolation source and NMDC BioSamples text. For each species, compare how much gene-content distance is explained by body-site labels versus embedding distance, after removing phylogenetic distance. Compare hosts with free-living species.
directions.title: Do host-associated bacteria track host body site rather than geography?
directions.why_it_matters: It would explain the null difference between lifestyles as a measurement error and show what environment variable matters for host-associated bacteria.

directions.hypothesis: Warming increases methane oxidation by raising pmoA activity per cell in existing methanotroph populations, with little change in their abundance.
directions.outcomes: Support: higher methane uptake and pmoA transcript-to-DNA ratios in heated soil with similar pmoA DNA. Refutation: uptake follows pmoA DNA abundance, or heated soils show no uptake difference.
directions.prior_work: PMID 38561130 saw higher methane uptake with warming but no rise in pmoA copies in DNA, and PMID 34512564 profiled warming RNA without these genes; this tests the activity-versus-abundance explanation directly.
directions.question: In long-term heated forest soil, methane-oxidation and glyoxylate-cycle transcripts rose under warming in suggestive signals, Actinobacteria rose and Acidobacteria fell, yet the RNA pool was no more warming-sensitive than DNA. Is warming activating a subset of existing organisms?
directions.readiness_basis: Existing data come from one timepoint and the methane-oxidation signals were only suggestive once the many genes tested were taken into account, so new sampling is required.
directions.test: Measure methane uptake and pmoA DNA and RNA from heated and control Harvard Forest soils, both organic and mineral horizons, at several seasons. Include labelled-methane incubations to identify active methanotrophs. Relate transcript-to-DNA ratios to uptake rates. Check in NMDC Multi-omics warming datasets whether pmoA carriers are recovered as genomes.
directions.title: Does warming raise methane oxidation by activating existing methanotrophs rather than growing them?
directions.why_it_matters: It would show that warming responses can occur without community turnover, which affects how soil methane sinks are forecast.

directions.hypothesis: ExoS-positive CF isolates form CF-specific clades with more accessory-gene divergence from environmental strains, while ExoU-positive CF isolates sit inside environmental clades.
directions.outcomes: Support: ExoU-positive CF isolates are nested in environmental clades and ExoS-positive isolates form CF-dominated clades. Refutation: both groups are equally mixed with environmental relatives.
directions.prior_work: PMID 19936230 found nearly all CF strains ExoS-positive in a 328-isolate panel, and PMID 42151817 describes co-colonising ExoU and ExoS strains; this asks about origin and adaptation history across thousands of genomes.
directions.question: Most cystic fibrosis Pseudomonas aeruginosa isolates carry the ExoS toxin gene, whereas environmental isolates are far more often ExoU-positive. Are the ExoU-positive CF isolates recent environmental immigrants and the ExoS-positive ones long-adapted lung lineages?
directions.readiness_basis: Effector typing and isolation labels exist for thousands of genomes, but a tree-based comparison has not been done.
directions.test: Using the Pangenome Collection and PROTECT Pathogen Browser, build a core-genome tree for the Pseudomonas aeruginosa genomes with environmental metadata. Classify each by effector type and isolation source. Test whether ExoU-positive CF isolates have nearest relatives from environmental sources more often than ExoS-positive CF isolates, and compare accessory gene divergence from the nearest environmental relative.
directions.title: Are ExoU-carrying cystic fibrosis Pseudomonas recent arrivals from the environment?
directions.why_it_matters: It would show that toxin type marks adaptation history and that results from the ExoU-positive PA14 strain may not apply to typical CF infections.

directions.hypothesis: Genes that stay dark after reannotation mostly encode functions used in nutrient scavenging and microbe-microbe interaction, so their strong phenotypes shift toward mixed-community and iron conditions. Single-organism stress screens will keep missing them.
directions.outcomes: Support: under both reported comparisons, and within condition-matched organisms, dark genes shift away from stress, and their phenotypes concentrate in co-culture and iron conditions. Refute: the shift disappears once organisms are matched for condition coverage, or co-culture adds no dark-gene phenotypes beyond those of annotated genes.
directions.prior_work: PMID 29769716 and PMID 22125499 tie poorly annotated genes to conditions but do not contrast persistently dark genes with annotation-lag genes by condition type. This direction tests an interaction-function explanation that neither paper examines.
directions.question: Genes still unannotated after reannotation had fewer strong stress phenotypes than genes that merely lacked an annotation: 28.7% vs 43.2% in one comparison and 43.3% vs 54.7% in another, and the two pairs of figures have not been reconciled. Do these genes act in microbial interaction and iron scavenging rather than stress defence?
directions.readiness_basis: The within-organism comparison uses existing fitness data. Testing interaction functions needs new co-culture screens, since the Fitness Browser has few mixed-community experiments.
directions.test: First, in the Fitness Browser, recompute both reported stress comparisons from the same gene sets, so the two pairs of figures are kept side by side and not treated as one settled result. Restrict to organisms with comparable numbers of stress, nutrient, iron and mixed-community experiments, and ask whether the shift away from stress holds within organisms. Then run barcoded-transposon fitness screens of a deeply profiled organism in monoculture versus defined co-culture with an Oak Ridge groundwater partner, and score whether dark genes gain strong effects specifically in co-culture. Use the Pangenome Collection to check whether co-culture-dependent genes are accessory and narrow in ortholog breadth.
directions.title: Do dark genes that resist reannotation work through community interactions rather than stress?
directions.why_it_matters: One project found that stress conditions dominate strong dark-gene phenotypes. Another found the hardest-to-annotate genes depleted in stress. If these genes are interaction functions, stress panels are the wrong way to characterise them and experimental prioritisation should change.

directions.hypothesis: Core proteins with shallow sequence families are more often essential or strongly condition-dependent than deep-family core proteins of similar length. Their conservation then reflects selection on lineage-restricted functions, not sampling bias.
directions.outcomes: Support: after length matching and member-level depth checks, shallow core genes show more essentiality or condition-specific defects in several lineages. Refute: they look like deep core genes once length is controlled, or the enrichment appears only in the over-sampled genera or only with representative-sequence depth.
directions.prior_work: PMID 41273079 and PMID 34791371 describe structure coverage of sequence space, and PMID 29769716 reports phenotypes for poorly annotated genes. None asks whether shallow sequence families among conserved genes are enriched for essential functions.
directions.question: Hundreds of thousands of core gene clusters have very shallow sequence families and are rarely annotated with an enzyme or pathway. Does their conservation reflect essential or condition-critical roles in their lineages, or is it an artefact of over-sampled genera and of depth measured on one representative sequence?
directions.readiness_basis: The low-depth core cluster list and fitness data both exist, but the join of cluster representatives to Fitness Browser genes has not been run and member-level depth must be computed.
directions.test: Map the shallow-family core clusters to Fitness Browser genes through the Pangenome Collection and compare essentiality and strong condition-specific fitness with deep-family core clusters. Depth was looked up only for each cluster's representative sequence, so recompute depth for the fitness-tested gene itself and for several members, and drop clusters where these disagree. Match on gene length, because short genes get fewer transposon insertions. Repeat within Pseudomonas and E. coli separately and in less sampled lineages, since these genera are over-represented. Follow up with knockdown phenotyping of a few top candidates in E. coli K-12.
directions.title: Are widely conserved core proteins with very shallow sequence families quietly essential?
directions.why_it_matters: If shallow core proteins are disproportionately essential, they are the best-justified targets for structure-based function discovery. If not, the conserved-yet-novel population is largely a sampling artefact and the unannotated core is smaller than it looks.

directions.hypothesis: SNIPE-family proteins are retained mainly in genomes that encode ManYZ and are lost or rarer in related genomes lacking it, because the defence only has a target where phage entry goes through that transporter.
directions.outcomes: Support: within genera, confirmed SNIPE tracks ManYZ presence, and in Klebsiella SNIPE protection against ManYZ-dependent phages disappears in manYZ-deleted hosts. Refute: SNIPE occurs equally in hosts with and without ManYZ, and protection does not depend on the transporter.
directions.prior_work: PMID 41741653 shows a membrane nuclease cleaving phage DNA during injection, and PMID 34032565 reports membrane-level defences in E. coli. Neither relates the defence's distribution across species to the presence of the phage-entry transporter.
directions.question: The SNIPE membrane nuclease defence domain occurs across dozens of bacterial and archaeal phyla, and SNIPE-bearing species differ from others in environmental embeddings. Is its retention tied to hosts that carry the mannose transporter ManYZ, which phages use for DNA entry?
directions.readiness_basis: The co-occurrence analysis can use existing domain annotations, but Klebsiella has no fitness tables or phage-receptor data, so the decisive phage-challenge test needs new mutant libraries and phage screening.
directions.test: Only an estimated 80.4% of domain-positive clusters are SNIPE-family proteins, and only 54 of 4,572 show the expected nuclease domain, so first restrict to clusters with a confirmed SNIPE-type nuclease domain or a sequence-based family call and keep the domain-only set as a comparison. In the Pangenome Collection, test within genera whether SNIPE presence co-occurs with ManYZ presence. Experimentally, build transposon mutant libraries in SNIPE-carrying Klebsiella pneumoniae strains (NCTC9140 or HS11286), where no fitness data exist. Choose phages by empirical screening of a panel on manYZ-deleted versus intact hosts, since the Klebsiella browser holds genome annotations only and gives no phage-receptor data. Then test whether SNIPE loss lets ManYZ-dependent phages replicate, and whether manYZ loss makes SNIPE dispensable.
directions.title: Does SNIPE persist only where phages enter through the mannose transporter?
directions.why_it_matters: A coupling between a defence and one receptor would show that defence repertoires are tailored to receptor use, and would predict which hosts are protected. Absence of coupling would mean the broad phylum spread reflects other targets or mechanisms.

directions.hypothesis: Within genera where the PHB synthase gene is accessory, carrier strains come from more variable or nutrient-pulsed environments than their non-carrier relatives. Acquisition of the gene tracks habitat variability, not inherited lineage.
directions.outcomes: Support: within-genus carriers come from more variable habitats, and the deletion mutant survives starvation cycles worse than wild type. Refute: carriers and non-carriers within genera come from similar habitats, and the mutant survives cycles as well as wild type.
directions.prior_work: PMID 24887088 and PMID 17113245 infer transfer of PHB genes from phylogeny or gene organisation, and PMID 42203387 links PHB to fluctuating environments across the tree of life. None compares habitats of carrier and non-carrier strains within a lineage.
directions.question: Polyhydroxybutyrate (PHB) carbon storage is more common in species from variable environments, and the pattern holds in every genome-size group. Among species that carry the PHB synthase gene as an accessory gene, do carrier strains come from more variable habitats than non-carrier relatives, which would point to adaptive acquisition?
directions.readiness_basis: Gene presence, accessory status and environment metadata exist in the lakehouse, but the within-genus comparison has not been run and metadata is sparse for many genomes.
directions.test: In the Pangenome Collection, select genera in which the PHB synthase gene is accessory in at least some species. Compare habitat variability between carrier and non-carrier genomes within the same species or genus, using isolation-source metadata. Then test the mechanism in an organism like Pseudomonas extremaustralis, where the gene has both horizontally acquired and core copies: compare survival of the wild type and a deletion mutant under repeated cycles of nutrient pulse and starvation.
directions.title: Is storage polymer production acquired by transfer to survive feast-and-famine habitats?
directions.why_it_matters: The overall PHB-niche link was shown to be confounded by genome size, so it cannot yet support the feast-and-famine idea. A within-genus link between habitat and gene gain would test the idea in a way lineage and genome size cannot explain.

directions.hypothesis: Quinate growth produces a short-lived NADH surge that exceeds the alternative dehydrogenase's capacity, so Complex I deletion fails on quinate but not on glucose. Raising alternative dehydrogenase activity should rescue the Complex I mutant on quinate.
directions.outcomes: Support: a transient NADH rise on quinate and rescue of the Complex I mutant by extra dehydrogenase capacity. Refute: NADH levels on quinate match glucose and extra dehydrogenase does not rescue the mutant, pointing to another cause such as proton-motive-force demand.
directions.prior_work: PMID 18319726 phenotyped the ADP1 deletion collection and PMID 25374488 described quinate-specific expression changes. Neither tests an NADH-burst explanation for Complex I dependence.
directions.question: In Acinetobacter baylyi ADP1, Complex I matters on quinate even though quinate yields less NADH per carbon than glucose or acetate. Is the reason that ring cleavage releases NADH in a burst that the alternative NADH dehydrogenase cannot reoxidise quickly enough?
directions.readiness_basis: The existing data are growth ratios and protein abundance; the NADH-burst explanation rests on theoretical stoichiometry and needs new redox and genetic measurements.
directions.test: Measure the NADH-to-NAD+ ratio over time in wild-type ADP1 grown on quinate, glucose and acetate, looking for a transient peak on quinate. Express a strong non-proton-pumping NADH dehydrogenase in a Complex I deletion strain and test growth on quinate. Separately, add an NDH-2 deletion to test compensation on glucose, since that gene has no growth data in the existing collection. Extend to species that carry and lack the aromatic degradation pathway by checking co-retention of Complex I in the Pangenome Collection.
directions.title: Does a burst of NADH on quinate make Complex I indispensable?
directions.why_it_matters: It would show that respiratory requirements follow the rate of reducing-equivalent release from a pathway and not its total yield. That is a different kind of rule for predicting which respiratory components a metabolic route needs.

directions.hypothesis: As a hypothesis, lipid A loss is tolerated only when fur loss and preserved expression of the cbb3/fix respiratory operon coincide. Either change alone fails, and forcing cbb3 expression substitutes for the sspB deletion.
directions.outcomes: Support: lpxC deletion is lethal in either single background and viable in fur-only with forced cbb3 expression. Refute: fur-only is enough for viability, or cbb3 expression does not substitute for sspB loss, consistent with the null fitness result for these genes. Lipidomics separately tells whether the sphingolipid pool is maintained.
directions.prior_work: PMID 35649364 shows fur mutations and anionic sphingolipids make lipid A dispensable, and PMID 19520766 and PMID 30210482 define the Fur regulon. None tests a respiratory-operon requirement or an sspB-linked buffering effect.
directions.question: Caulobacter can lose lipid A when the iron regulator Fur is absent, and the rescued strain also lacks sspB. Loss of sspB buffers the Fur-dependent micro-aerobic respiratory operon at transcript level, and sphingolipid biosynthesis genes are not switched on in routine rich medium. Does rescue require the respiratory buffering as well as fur loss?
directions.readiness_basis: The transcript buffering and the absence of sphingolipid gene induction in rich medium are measured, but their causal role in rescue has not been tested, and iron-limitation fitness data are missing.
directions.test: In Caulobacter, test viability of the lpxC deletion in a fur-only background and an sspB-only background. Then express the cbb3/fix operon from an independent promoter in the fur-only background and ask whether it restores viability. Measure sphingolipid levels by lipidomics in the rescued strain, to learn whether the pool is maintained without gene induction, which the transcript data alone cannot show. Fitness data did not distinguish the buffered respiratory set from background, so check in new envelope-stress fitness experiments whether these genes matter at all.
directions.title: Does lipid A loss in Caulobacter need both Fur release and a preserved respiratory operon?
directions.why_it_matters: It would explain why a single regulator mutation permits loss of an essential outer-membrane lipid, and would link envelope remodelling to oxygen-linked respiration. The existing data show the respiratory buffering but do not show that it matters for rescue, so this tests whether it does.

directions.hypothesis: The dark Methanococcus genes are conserved within methanogens but absent from other archaea and bacteria. They also show phenotypes under methanogen-specific conditions such as nitrogen source and metal limitation, which marks them as lineage innovations.
directions.outcomes: Support: the genes are restricted to methanogens and gain strong phenotypes under methanogen-relevant nutrient or metal conditions. Refute: they have orthologs in annotated non-methanogen lineages, or show no condition-specific phenotypes.
directions.prior_work: PMID 39120137 identifies nutrient-utilisation genes in a model methanogen by high-throughput genetics, and PMID 42706541 benchmarks annotation tools across species. Neither asks whether archaeal dark genes are lineage-specific innovations.
directions.question: Methanococcus strains account for most of the genes that stay unannotated after reannotation. Are these genes real methanogen-specific functions, instead of genes that look dark because reference databases cover archaea poorly?
directions.readiness_basis: Ortholog breadth and existing fitness conditions can be analysed now, but the metal conditions for Methanococcus have not been measured.
directions.test: In the Pangenome Collection, trace ortholog breadth of the dark Methanococcus genes across archaeal and bacterial genomes. In the Fitness Browser, check which conditions give them strong effects, and use cofitness to place them in operons with annotated genes. Then run the proposed metal panel (nickel, cobalt, copper, zinc, tungsten and molybdenum) on Methanococcus maripaludis S2 and JJ, which carry metal candidates but only iron fitness data, and score the dark genes.
directions.title: Are archaeal dark genes methanogen-specific innovations rather than annotation lag?
directions.why_it_matters: If so, the apparent excess of dark genes in archaea reflects unique biology that annotation transfer from bacteria cannot reach, and calls for archaeal-specific experiments. If they are database-coverage artefacts, they would resolve with better archaeal references.

directions.hypothesis: Genes lethal when fully deleted but tolerated by transposon insertion carry their insertions mostly near the 3' end or between domains, leaving a truncated protein that still works. Insertions in the same genes placed early in the coding sequence should reproduce the lethality.
directions.outcomes: Support: discordant genes have insertions concentrated late in the gene or after the key domains, and early insertions are lethal. Refute: insertion positions look like those of concordant genes and early insertions are also tolerated, which points to other explanations such as fitness costs without lethality.
directions.prior_work: PMID 18319726 built the ADP1 deletion collection but did not examine why transposon screens disagree with it, and PMID 25968644 describes the transposon method without testing partial-function insertions.
directions.question: In Acinetobacter baylyi ADP1, why do transposon-insertion fitness calls disagree so strongly with complete-deletion essentiality in rich medium? Do insertions leave partly functional gene products, or does something else explain the mismatch?
directions.readiness_basis: Both assay datasets exist for ADP1, but insertion-level positions and the early-insertion strains are not confirmed as available in the lakehouse.
directions.test: Using the ADP1 rich-medium datasets, map each insertion position and the retained protein domains for genes lethal when deleted but called dispensable by transposon screening. Compare against genes where the two assays agree. Then build a small set of early-position insertions and full deletions for about 20 discordant genes and compare growth in rich medium.
directions.title: Do partly working truncated proteins let transposon screens miss knockout-lethal ADP1 genes?
directions.why_it_matters: Transposon screens underpin essential-gene lists across many bacteria. If truncation is the main cause of misses, essential-gene catalogues are systematically biased toward genes with tolerable C-terminal truncations, and screens could be redesigned to account for this.

directions.hypothesis: Accessory genes lag behind core genes in showing condition-specific fitness effects under nutrient and chemical conditions, but the lag shrinks under interaction-type conditions such as mixed-community growth.
directions.outcomes: Support: the accessory shortfall shrinks or disappears in interaction-type classes. Refute: the shortfall is the same size in every class, which favours measurement bias or a genuine lack of effect. If too few interaction-type experiments exist, the question cannot be answered with current data and needs new screens.
directions.prior_work: PMID 29769716 reports condition-specific phenotypes for poorly annotated genes but does not split them by core versus accessory status or by interaction conditions.
directions.question: Genes with condition-specific phenotypes are more often core than accessory, and singleton genes look neutral in lab screens. Is that because most tested conditions are chemical or nutrient, while accessory genes may matter mainly in interactions such as mixed communities?
directions.readiness_basis: Fitness data and pangenome links exist, but the number of interaction-type experiments per organism is not stated and may be small.
directions.test: First count, per organism, how many Fitness Browser experiments are interaction-type (for example mixed-community growth) versus chemical or nutrient; the test proceeds only for organisms with enough of each. Then, per class, compute the share of core, accessory and singleton genes with strong condition-specific effects, linking genes through the Pangenome Collection and controlling for gene length and insertion coverage.
directions.title: Do accessory genes show fitness effects mainly under interaction conditions rather than chemical conditions?
directions.why_it_matters: It would show that the apparent lab neutrality of accessory genes reflects a gap in the tested conditions rather than true uselessness, and tell screen designers which condition classes to add.

directions.hypothesis: Among costly dispensable genes, those with condition-specific fitness effects are present in a larger fraction of genomes within their species than those without, a pattern that would be consistent with, though not proof of, slower gene loss.
directions.outcomes: Support: genes with condition-specific effects have higher within-species prevalence even after removing mobile-element genes. Refute: prevalence is the same in both groups. Because the comparison is cross-sectional, support would motivate, not establish, a slower loss rate.
directions.prior_work: PMID 22448042 and PMID 22761588 predict loss of costly dispensable genes but do not test whether condition-specific fitness effects relate to retention in measured fitness data.
directions.question: Some genes cost fitness in the lab and are dispensable, yet a share still have condition-specific fitness effects. Are such genes found in a larger fraction of their species' genomes than costly dispensable genes without such effects?
directions.readiness_basis: The costly dispensable classes and their condition-specific phenotypes already exist and the pangenome links are established.
directions.test: In the Fitness Browser, classify genes as costly dispensable with or without condition-specific fitness effects. Map them to the Pangenome Collection and compare within-species prevalence, controlling for gene length, mobile-element annotation and organism. Repeat after excluding genes annotated as transposase, integrase or phage, which dominate the costly dispensable class.
directions.title: Do costly dispensable genes with condition-specific fitness effects persist in more genomes?
directions.why_it_matters: It would link lab fitness trade-offs to how widely costly genes are retained, giving a data-based test of the Black Queen idea that costly genes are shed unless they sometimes matter.

directions.hypothesis: Most essential-auxiliary genes lie within or beside mobile elements and are absent, without a core replacement, in close relatives lacking the element, consistent with addiction rather than compensation.
directions.outcomes: Support: most such genes sit in mobile-element neighbourhoods and lack core replacements. Refute: they are largely independent of mobile elements and sit where a core counterpart is missing in the host.
directions.prior_work: PMID 33760724 ties non-core essential genes to mobile elements in Xanthomonas, and PMID 36097170 shows strain-dependent essentiality in one species. Neither tests compensation versus addiction across many organisms.
directions.question: Thousands of genes are essential yet found only in some genomes, and many are hypothetical or belong to replication, secretion and plasmid systems. Are they essential because they are strain-specific stand-ins for core machinery, or because they sit in mobile elements that make the host dependent on them?
directions.readiness_basis: Essential-auxiliary gene sets and pangenome links exist, but genomic-context extraction across 33 organisms has not been done.
directions.test: For the essential-auxiliary genes across the 33 organisms, use the Pangenome Collection and KBase Genomes to find neighbouring mobile-element and toxin-antitoxin genes. In relatives lacking the element, test whether a core paralog performs the same function. Validate in one tractable organism by CRISPR knockdown of a few examples.
directions.title: Are essential-auxiliary genes essential through mobile-element addiction rather than compensating for core gaps?
directions.why_it_matters: It separates two reasons for strain-dependent essentiality: filling a core gap versus dependence on parasitic DNA, which changes how essential genes are used as drug targets or minimal-genome candidates.

directions.hypothesis: The strength of essential-gene core enrichment declines with pangenome openness across organisms, even after matching the number of genomes per species.
directions.outcomes: Support: enrichment weakens steadily as openness rises after genome-count matching. Refute: enrichment is unrelated to openness, leaving thin sampling or biology unrelated to pangenome structure as explanations.
directions.prior_work: PMID 36097170, PMID 39012116 and PMID 42348439 describe core and strain-specific essential genes within single species or genera, and PMID 38948139 relates fitness to core status in one species. None relates enrichment strength to pangenome openness across organisms.
directions.question: Essential genes are only modestly more often core than other genes, and the enrichment is clearly present in only about half the organisms. Does the enrichment fade in species with open, diverse pangenomes, where strains may supply essential functions through accessory genes?
directions.readiness_basis: Per-organism enrichment results and pangenome tables exist; only the openness comparison across organisms is new.
directions.test: For each of the 33 organisms, take the essential-gene core enrichment from the Fitness Browser linked to the Pangenome Collection. Compute openness on genome-count-matched resamples and compare with enrichment across organisms, adding lineage as a covariate. Examine the organisms with no enrichment individually.
directions.title: Does an open pangenome weaken the link between essentiality and core status?
directions.why_it_matters: It would explain why conservation is a poor essentiality predictor in some lineages and show that essentiality depends on pangenome structure, guiding when conservation can be used to flag drug targets.

directions.hypothesis: The urea defects are mostly nitrogen-specific: when growth rate is matched with a slow, non-urea nitrogen condition, a compact set of nitrogen-handling genes stays defective on urea while the broad defect fraction falls.
directions.outcomes: Support: the broad defect fraction drops in the growth-matched control and the retained urea-only genes form a compact nitrogen-related set. Refute: the broad defect fraction persists in the slow control, showing a growth-rate effect rather than a urea-specific requirement.
directions.prior_work: PMID 18319726 phenotyped the ADP1 deletion collection on several carbon sources and PMID 25374488 studied quinate-specific expression changes. Neither tests whether growth rate drives the demand tiers.
directions.question: In the ADP1 deletion collection, nearly all genes show severe defects on urea but few on quinate, and urea behaves largely independently of the carbon sources. Does urea reveal a distinct nitrogen-metabolism gene set, or does slow growth on it magnify every defect?
directions.readiness_basis: The existing data is a single set of 8 conditions, with no nitrogen-source or growth-rate-matched comparison.
directions.test: Grow the ADP1 deletion collection on urea as nitrogen source and on a non-urea nitrogen source at the same carbon source, plus a slow-growth control condition chosen to match the urea growth rate. Compare the defect fractions and identify genes defective on urea but not in the growth-matched control; compare them with the genes specific to urea in the existing data.
directions.title: Is the near-universal urea defect a nitrogen-metabolism requirement or a slow-growth effect?
directions.why_it_matters: It would tell whether the demanding tier reports real nitrogen-source requirements or a growth-rate threshold, which determines how condition-specific gene sets from deletion collections should be read.

directions.hypothesis: The shared metal and NaCl genes respond to osmotic pressure or envelope damage rather than to a specific ion. Metal overlap with non-ionic osmotic conditions should then match overlap with NaCl, and should not depend on how much chloride the metal salt delivers.
directions.outcomes: Support for an osmotic cause: overlap with sorbitol-type conditions is as high as with NaCl at every cutoff, while envelope conditions add little. Support for envelope damage: the reverse. Refute both: overlap is specific to NaCl or KCl, or vanishes with non-ionic conditions, pointing to an ion-specific mechanism. A result that changes with the cutoff or experiment count would be inconclusive.
directions.prior_work: PMID 32986214 reports copper and zinc growth inhibition without separating ion from osmotic effects. PMID 25968644 and PMID 29769716 supply the fitness method and data. This direction asks what the shared fitness signal responds to.
directions.question: Many genes that matter under metal stress also matter under NaCl, even for zinc delivered as sulfate with no chloride. Is the shared stress osmotic pressure, envelope damage, or something specific to sodium or chloride?
directions.readiness_basis: Metal and NaCl experiments already exist in the Fitness Browser. Which non-ionic osmotic and envelope experiments exist per organism is not stated, so coverage may limit the first step.
directions.test: In the Fitness Browser, take the 19 organisms with metal and NaCl experiments. Run two separate comparisons: (a) each metal's gene overlap with non-ionic osmotic conditions (sugar or polyol), and (b) overlap with envelope-targeting conditions, each set against overlap with NaCl. Within each organism, subsample to equal numbers of experiments per condition type, and repeat at several cutoffs for calling a gene important, since the overlap depends on that cutoff. Compare chloride-delivering metals (cobalt, copper, nickel) with sulfate-delivered zinc. Then, in Desulfovibrio vulgaris Hildenborough, run barcoded transposon fitness assays with matched chloride and sulfate salts, KCl and sorbitol.
directions.title: Is the overlap between metal and salt fitness caused by osmotic stress or by envelope damage?
directions.why_it_matters: It would show what the shared-stress component of metal fitness data actually measures. Metal-specific genes could then be separated from general damage responses, and metal fitness could be read mechanistically.

directions.hypothesis: If organisms in the Fitness Browser are limited to 8 carbon-source experiments, their module structure will collapse into a continuous gradient like ADP1's. The way ADP1 was perturbed, by single deletion rather than pooled transposon mutants, then matters little.
directions.outcomes: Support: 8-condition subsamples lose most modules and look like ADP1 in both the lakehouse and the pooled ADP1 library. Refute: 8-condition subsamples keep distinct modules, or pooled ADP1 data show modules the deletion screen missed. That would point to perturbation type or ADP1 biology.
directions.prior_work: PMID 18319726 built the ADP1 deletion collection and PMID 38323821 decomposed transposon fitness data for Pseudomonas putida. PMID 29545622 benchmarked module detection methods. None separates condition number from perturbation type.
directions.question: A deletion screen of Acinetobacter baylyi ADP1 on 8 carbon sources found a continuous gradient with one discrete 24-gene quinate module. Cross-organism analyses of transposon data recover many coherent modules. Is the difference due to the number of conditions, or to the kind of perturbation?
directions.readiness_basis: The subsampling uses existing Fitness Browser data. The ADP1 pooled library is a new experiment, since ADP1 is absent from that dataset.
directions.test: For each Fitness Browser organism with many carbon-source experiments, repeatedly draw 8 carbon-source experiments. Group genes with the clustering method the ADP1 study used, and also with independent component analysis (a method that splits a gene-by-condition table into sets of genes whose fitness rises and falls together, called modules). Record how much discrete module structure remains and compare it with ADP1's weak clustering and single small aromatic module. Then build a pooled transposon library of ADP1, grow it on the same 8 carbon sources, and analyze it the same way.
directions.title: Is ADP1's smooth phenotype landscape caused by having only eight conditions?
directions.why_it_matters: It would show whether module calls from one dataset reflect biology or experimental design. That tells researchers how many conditions are needed before gene groups can be read as organized units.

directions.hypothesis: Genes for iron-sulfur cluster assembly and repair carry most of the iron-zinc shared fitness. Removing them should collapse the overlap, and extra iron should relieve zinc sensitivity in their mutants.
directions.outcomes: Support: iron-sulfur genes hold a disproportionate share of the shared signal, and iron supplementation rescues their zinc sensitivity. Refute: the shared signal is spread across unrelated functions, or iron does not rescue.
directions.prior_work: PMID 31586033 shows zinc excess raises the iron demand of E. coli, and PMID 37272830 links iron uptake to zinc responses in a single organism. This direction tests the iron-sulfur cluster explanation across organisms with a gene-level prediction.
directions.question: Iron and zinc showed unexpectedly strong shared fitness effects across 6 organisms. Does zinc excess act on iron-sulfur cluster proteins, so that genes for building and repairing those clusters drive the shared signal?
directions.readiness_basis: Iron and zinc fitness data exist for 6 organisms. The rescue experiment needs new measurements.
directions.test: In the 6 organisms with both iron and zinc experiments in the Fitness Browser, mark iron-sulfur assembly, repair and iron-sulfur-enzyme genes. Compare how much of the iron-zinc shared signal sits in them against matched sets of genes with similar overall fitness and conservation. Then, in one organism, grow clean deletions of the assembly genes with zinc, with and without added iron, and measure growth.
directions.title: Do zinc and iron stress overlap because both damage iron-sulfur cluster proteins?
directions.why_it_matters: It would explain a cross-organism pattern with a specific cellular mechanism. It would also show that the metal overlap is more than generic stress.

directions.hypothesis: Families found in some bioleaching genera and rare in matched non-bioleaching relatives will also separate bioleaching genera that were not used to find them, and will do so better than the broad signature score.
directions.outcomes: Support: a small family set found in one genus separates held-out specialists from their relatives better than the broad signature. Refute: families found in one genus fail on held-out genera, so specialists look like other species. That would suggest tolerance relies on regulation or sequence variants invisible to gene content.
directions.prior_work: PMID 30389769 and PMID 12829273 describe metal-resistance genes in Acidithiobacillus. PMID 29150517 and PMID 27712915 describe acidophile genomes. None tests whether specialist-specific families, rather than repertoire size, separate specialists in held-out genera.
directions.question: Bioleaching genera were not enriched as a group for a broad metal gene signature once genome size was accounted for, though Leptospirillum ranked high on its own. Do these specialists tolerate metals through a few distinct gene families rather than a bigger general repertoire?
directions.readiness_basis: Pangenome and Fitness Browser data are in the lakehouse. Matched comparison sets need building, and only a few bioleaching genera have pangenomes, which limits held-out rotation.
directions.test: In the Pangenome Collection, find gene families enriched in one bioleaching genus (for example Acidithiobacillus) against matched non-bioleaching relatives. Test them only on held-out bioleaching genera (for example Leptospirillum) and their matched relatives, rotating which genus is held out. Use the literature-based bioleaching status of each genus as the label, not any property of the discovery set. Compare with the broad signature score. Check overlap with the 149 conserved but unannotated metal-phenotype families from the Fitness Browser and whether the families carry metal-related annotations.
directions.title: Do extreme metal-tolerant bacteria rely on a few specialist gene families rather than breadth?
directions.why_it_matters: It would show that species-level metal scores built from long gene lists miss real specialists. Searches for metal-tolerant organisms could then target specific families.

directions.hypothesis: Efflux gene mutants change their antibiotic sensitivity when histidine or tryptophan availability changes. This reflects metabolic control of efflux, not shared lab dispensability.
directions.outcomes: Support: efflux mutant sensitivity shifts with amino-acid supply and the biosynthesis neighbours explain it. Refute: sensitivity does not change with supplementation, so the neighbourhood is shared dispensability.
directions.prior_work: PMID 21645016 reviews metabolic regulation of resistance and PMID 39038993 shows tryptophan transport loss promotes resistance. Neither tests efflux genes against biosynthesis cofitness neighbours.
directions.question: Efflux genes had cofitness neighbours enriched in histidine biosynthesis in 6 organisms and tryptophan biosynthesis in 5, while metal-resistance genes showed a weaker version of this. The apparent difference between efflux and metal-resistance genes was only a hint and was not firm once the many comparisons were accounted for. Does amino-acid metabolism set how efflux genes act?
directions.readiness_basis: Cofitness is in the Fitness Browser. Amino-acid supplementation contrasts may be sparse, so new assays are likely needed.
directions.test: Take efflux genes with biosynthesis neighbours in the Fitness Browser organisms where both were found. Use conditions with and without histidine or tryptophan to see whether efflux fitness shifts with supplementation more than for non-efflux genes of similar overall fitness. Then, in one organism, measure efflux mutants and biosynthesis mutants for sensitivity to a substrate antibiotic at graded amino-acid levels.
directions.title: Are efflux pumps tied to amino-acid biosynthesis through the cell's metabolic state?
directions.why_it_matters: It would tie resistance to nutrient state, which affects how resistance is treated or predicted. A null would show that the enrichment reflects shared dispensability.

directions.hypothesis: Iron acquisition and PQQ mutants fail on quinate because quinate dehydrogenase needs PQQ and ring cleavage needs iron. Added iron or PQQ should relieve the defects.
directions.outcomes: Support: iron or PQQ restores quinate growth in the matching mutants and the genes co-occur with the pathway. Refute: supplementation does not rescue, or the mutants are equally impaired on non-aromatic carbon.
directions.prior_work: PMID 3044290 and PMID 2855587 describe the PQQ-dependent quinate dehydrogenase, and PMID 8002591 and PMID 15691962 map the pathway genes. None addresses the iron and PQQ support set found by cofitness.
directions.question: Most genes with quinate-specific defects in ADP1 fall into four groups: the aromatic degradation pathway, Complex I, iron acquisition and PQQ biosynthesis. Do the iron and PQQ genes matter because quinate catabolism depends on an iron-containing enzyme and a PQQ-dependent dehydrogenase?
directions.readiness_basis: The co-occurrence step uses pangenome data. The rescue test needs ADP1 deletion mutants and new growth measurements.
directions.test: Grow deletions of the 7 iron acquisition genes and 2 PQQ biosynthesis genes in ADP1 on quinate with and without surplus iron or PQQ. Include growth on a non-aromatic carbon source as a control. Across the Pangenome Collection, ask whether species carrying the quinate pathway also keep iron-acquisition and PQQ genes more often than those without it.
directions.title: Does quinate need iron and PQQ support genes because its enzymes are iron- and cofactor-limited?
directions.why_it_matters: It would explain why the aromatic module has dispersed support genes. It would also show which co-factor supply limits growth on aromatics.

directions.hypothesis: A family is dispensable in an organism that carries a paralog or an alternative route, and essential in organisms that lack one. This should hold after accounting for growth medium, library depth and insertion bias.
directions.outcomes: Support: dispensability tracks backup presence, predicts it beyond relatedness and after the library controls, and knockdowns behave as predicted. Refute: backup presence is unrelated to variable essentiality once medium, depth and insertion bias are controlled, which would indicate that technical or condition differences drive the variation.
directions.prior_work: PMID 36097170 and PMID 42726091 describe strain-dependent essential genes within one species or family, and PMID 33753464 shows some ribosomal proteins are dispensable. None tests whether backup genes explain variable essentiality across many species.
directions.question: Of 17,222 ortholog families (groups of genes in different species descended from one ancestral gene) across 48 bacteria, 4,799 are essential in some organisms and not in others. Does a backup copy within the genome (a paralog, a related gene arising from duplication) or an alternative pathway explain why a family is essential in one organism and dispensable in another?
directions.readiness_basis: Essentiality calls and pangenome gene content are in the lakehouse. Paralog and pathway features need computing.
directions.test: For the variably essential families, compare organisms where the family is essential with those where it is not. Record paralog count and completeness of alternative pathways from pathway predictions, using Fitness Browser essentiality and the Pangenome Collection. Control for the growth medium of each library, the number of transposon insertions per library, gene length and insertion bias (short genes may look essential only because they lack insertions), by matching or adding them as covariates. Check whether backup presence predicts essentiality beyond phylogenetic relatedness. Then knock down predictable cases, such as ribosomal-protein families, in an organism lacking the backup and one carrying it.
directions.title: Are gene families essential in some bacteria but not others rescued by backup copies?
directions.why_it_matters: It would show that essentiality is set by genome context, not only by gene function. That would improve essential-gene prediction and drug-target choice.

directions.hypothesis: Resistance genes that are core are those whose products also serve non-antibiotic roles, such as envelope maintenance or stress handling. Within a mechanism class they should show fitness effects under non-antibiotic stresses and co-vary with non-resistance genes, whereas accessory ones should be functionally isolated.
directions.outcomes: Support: core resistance genes show more non-antibiotic phenotypes and stronger co-variation with envelope or regulatory genes than accessory ones of the same mechanism. Refute: the two groups look alike once mechanism is held fixed, which would point to mobility rather than physiological integration.
directions.prior_work: PMID 35873140 shows some efflux genes are core in one species and PMID 25861385 shows cost varies by drug class, but neither asks what non-antibiotic role could make a resistance gene permanent.
directions.question: Resistance mechanism strongly predicts whether a resistance gene is core or accessory, yet it does not predict knockout fitness cost. Intrinsic efflux pumps such as emhABC are more than 95% core, beta-lactamases are 54.9% core, regulatory genes are 6.5% core, and blaTEM, tet(C) and ant(2'')-Ia are 0% core. What besides cost explains this spread?
directions.readiness_basis: Resistance genes were already linked to fitness data and core status across 25 organisms, so the first step uses existing linked tables; the knockout step needs new measurements.
directions.test: The mechanism labels came from keyword matching on product descriptions, so first re-assign them from the gene annotations and check that the core-versus-accessory spread survives. Then, for resistance genes in Fitness Browser organisms with conservation status from the Pangenome Collection, compare core and accessory genes within each mechanism class. Measure (a) fitness under non-antibiotic stresses such as detergents, osmotic stress and metals, and (b) how closely each gene's fitness pattern tracks that of non-resistance genes across all experiments. Then knock out a core efflux operon such as emhABC in a host that carries it and test growth under envelope stress.
directions.title: Is a resistance gene's conservation set by how embedded it is in physiology?
directions.why_it_matters: It would separate resistance genes that are permanent parts of cell physiology from true add-ons. That changes which resistance genes can be targeted without side effects, and explains conservation without invoking cost.

directions.hypothesis: Resistance genes whose base and codon composition differs most from their host genome, an indirect hint of more recent acquisition, carry the highest cost, and cost shrinks as composition becomes host-like and prevalence within a species rises.
directions.outcomes: Support: cost falls steadily as composition becomes host-like, independent of singleton status. Refute: cost is flat across the composition gradient, or the singleton signal disappears when one gene-linking method is used for all classes.
directions.prior_work: PMID 25861385 and PMID 29439838 describe cost and compensation for resistance mutations, but they do not test whether the cost of native resistance genes decays with time since acquisition in genome-wide knockout data.
directions.question: Core and accessory resistance genes have identical baseline knockout fitness, yet a separate analysis finds that single-genome resistance genes are the costliest class. Is cost tied to how recently a gene arrived rather than to its core or accessory label?
directions.readiness_basis: Gene linking and fitness exist, but composition-deviation metrics must be computed from genome sequences.
directions.test: In Fitness Browser organisms with linked pangenomes, take each resistance gene's sequence from KBase Genomes and compute its deviation in base composition and codon usage from the host genome, together with within-species prevalence from the Pangenome Collection. Composition deviation is only a proxy and does not give acquisition history, so also check whether it separates singleton genes from widely shared ones. Ask whether baseline knockout fitness is predicted by the deviation among non-singleton genes as well as singletons. For a strain carrying a likely recent acquisition, run a competition assay between carrier and knockout strain without antibiotic.
directions.title: Do newly acquired resistance genes pay a cost that fades as they are integrated?
directions.why_it_matters: If true, cost is transient after acquisition, and the absent core-versus-accessory difference hides a time-dependent cost. That would help explain how resistance persists once acquired.

directions.hypothesis: Many of its costly dispensable genes are costly only in aerobic growth. They should lose their cost under anaerobic denitrifying conditions and be less rich in mobile-element annotations than the costly genes that stay costly.
directions.outcomes: Support: a large share of the costly set loses its cost anaerobically and is not mobile-element rich. Refute: cost persists across oxygen states and stays concentrated in transposase, phage and insertion-sequence genes, which favours genomic invasion.
directions.prior_work: PMID 32994326 shows gene dispensability depends on carbon environment in E. coli, and PMID 22448042 predicts loss of costly dispensable functions, but neither tests whether an outlier organism's costly set is an assay-mismatch effect.
directions.question: About a fifth of the genes in Pseudomonas stutzeri RCH2 (21.5%) are costly in the lab yet dispensable, far above the next organism (14.0%). Are they costly only because the lab differs from this denitrifier's natural anaerobic life, or do they reflect accumulation of costly mobile DNA?
directions.readiness_basis: The existing oxygen comparison in RCH2 is confounded with metal salt, so the decisive matched aerobic and anaerobic competition has to be newly measured.
directions.test: Existing aerobic and anaerobic experiments in RCH2 are confounded with the metal salt used, so they can only frame the question. Use the Fitness Browser to list RCH2's costly dispensable genes and compare mobile-element keyword enrichment and singleton share against the other costly genes. The decisive step is new: run pooled mutant competition in a defined medium under aerobic and anaerobic nitrate-reducing growth with no metal added, and see which genes change cost.
directions.title: Is one denitrifier's costly dispensable gene set a lab mismatch or mobile-DNA load?
directions.why_it_matters: It would show whether outlier organisms in cost surveys reveal real genomic parasitism or only a mismatch between assay and native lifestyle, which affects how lab-cost results are read as evidence for selection in nature.

directions.hypothesis: Metabolic ecotypes predict isolation environment better than core-genome subclade membership alone does, and pathways that vary within a species are those tied to nutrient sources of different habitats.
directions.outcomes: Support: ecotype labels carry environment information beyond what subclade labels carry, concentrated in nutrient-use pathways. Refute: environment is explained by subclade, or ecotype and environment are unrelated across species.
directions.prior_work: PMID 24465487 links metabolic flexibility to spatial distribution of communities and PMID 22928415 maps soil niche space by traits, but neither tests ecotypes inside species against isolation environment with phylogeny held fixed.
directions.question: Species with many genomes split into a handful of metabolic ecotypes by their pathway profiles. Do these ecotypes correspond to distinct isolation environments, or do they simply mirror subclades?
directions.readiness_basis: Pathway profiles and isolation metadata exist, but subclade structure and metadata harmonisation must be computed, and only a minority of genomes carry environmental embeddings.
directions.test: For the species with at least 50 genomes and variable pathways, cluster genomes by pathway profile in the Pangenome Collection. Score isolation-source categories using genome metadata, supplemented by NMDC BioSamples where strains link. Compare how well ecotype labels and core-genome subclade labels each predict isolation category within species, and whether the discriminating pathways are carbon or nitrogen utilization routes.
directions.title: Do the metabolic ecotypes within a bacterial species track where its strains live?
directions.why_it_matters: It would show that within-species metabolic variation is ecological adaptation rather than neutral drift, and give a way to infer habitat from genome content. The planned niche-breadth test for these ecotypes was never run.

directions.hypothesis: Metal-important genes involved in uptake, cofactor biosynthesis or metal-dependent enzymes are strongly core, while detoxification and efflux genes for metals with no biological role are much less core, so the pooled enrichment is a mixture of the two.
directions.outcomes: Support: uptake and cofactor genes are clearly more core than detoxification genes, and the difference between metal classes shrinks after the split. Refute: both gene types are similarly core, or toxic-only metals are as core-enriched as essential metals.
directions.prior_work: PMID 34765088 reports that most cadmium-responsive genes in one Enterococcus faecium strain are core, and PMID 34432491 and PMID 40302248 map metal-tolerance genes, but none separates essential-metal handling from toxicity defense when asking about conservation.
directions.question: Removing genes also important under salt stress left core-genome enrichment of metal-important genes intact, and strengthened it for essential metals; cadmium and iron, each in one organism, moved the other way. Do essential-metal use and acquisition genes carry the enrichment, while toxic-metal defense genes are as variable as other accessory genes?
directions.readiness_basis: Fitness data and core status already exist, but gene function labels must be assigned and the cadmium and iron results rest on one organism each.
directions.test: In Fitness Browser organisms with metal experiments, label each metal-important gene by annotation as uptake or cofactor use versus detoxification or efflux. Compare core fractions from the Pangenome Collection for each label, for essential metals (molybdenum, tungsten, selenium, nickel) versus toxic-only metals (mercury, cadmium, uranium), after removing genes also important under salt stress. Repeat with organisms contributing more than one metal to see whether the split holds within a genome.
directions.title: Does essential-metal cofactor handling, not toxicity defense, drive core enrichment of metal-fitness genes?
directions.why_it_matters: It would explain why different analyses disagree about whether metal genes are core or accessory, and show that conservation of metal fitness genes reflects ordinary physiology rather than adaptation to contaminated sites.

directions.hypothesis: Within genera that contain both soil/sediment and non-soil genomes, soil-derived genomes carry xoxF more often than their non-soil relatives, and inferred gain events fall more often on soil branches.
directions.outcomes: Support: a consistent soil excess within genera across several phyla, with gains concentrated on soil branches. Refutation: the excess disappears within genera, or appears in only one or two lineages, which points to lineage composition.
directions.prior_work: PMID 38369453 found xoxF gene clusters in Acidobacteria and other phyla from weathered granite and soil but did not test habitat against lineage; this asks whether habitat is associated with xoxF within lineages.
directions.question: Does the soil and sediment excess of xoxF persist when only close relatives are compared, so that it cannot be explained by which lineages happen to live in soil?
directions.readiness_basis: Genome and habitat data are in the lakehouse, but the within-genus tree building and gain/loss reconstruction need new computation.
directions.test: In the Pangenome Collection, take genera with genomes from both soil/sediment and other habitats, using habitat labels from NMDC BioSamples where available. Compare xoxF carriage between habitats within each genus. Build genus trees and reconstruct gain and loss to see whether gains map to soil branches. Repeat in several xoxF-carrying phyla, including Acidobacteriota, where the enrichment already survived a within-phylum comparison. Use annotations from both sources, since they disagree for xoxF. This is observational and can show association only. Selection would need a follow-up, such as lanthanide-limited growth of soil and non-soil relatives.
directions.title: Is soil habitat associated with xoxF gain inside single lineages, beyond lineage makeup?
directions.why_it_matters: A within-genus association would show that the soil signal is not only a by-product of methylotroph-rich lineages living in soil, and would justify testing selection directly. It would also show whether xoxF can serve as a habitat marker.

directions.hypothesis: Lanmodulin-positive genomes with xoxF confirmed absent carry other lanthanide-linked functions (for example other PQQ alcohol dehydrogenases) or come from lanthanide-rich habitats, so lanmodulin is retained for lanthanide handling independent of methanol oxidation.
directions.outcomes: Support: confirmed xoxF-free genomes consistently carry another lanthanide-linked enzyme or come from lanthanide-rich sources, and the deletion changes lanthanide-dependent growth or uptake. Refutation: xoxF is found in nearly all of them once better searches are used, or they carry no other partner, so lanmodulin simply tracks xoxF.
directions.prior_work: PMID 30351021 and 35814700 characterise lanmodulin in Methylobacterium and tie it to the lanthanide methanol dehydrogenase; PMID 41023737 surveys the lanthanome in methane oxidisers. None asks what lanmodulin does where xoxF is truly missing.
directions.question: Among lanmodulin-carrying genomes, those lacking an xoxF call may truly lack it or may reflect incomplete annotation. If sequence-level checks confirm xoxF is absent, do these genomes use lanthanides in other enzymes, or for storage or detoxification?
directions.readiness_basis: The genomic screen is feasible now, but the function test needs growth and metal-uptake work in a lanmodulin-positive, xoxF-free strain.
directions.test: Take the lanmodulin-positive genomes in Beijerinckiaceae, Acetobacteraceae and Hyphomicrobiaceae and flag those without an xoxF call from either annotation source. Confirm absence with a sequence-profile search for XoxF clades and an assembly completeness check, and keep only confirmed-absent genomes. Search that group in UniProt Annotations and UniRef Clusters for other PQQ-dependent dehydrogenases and for genes neighbouring lanmodulin, and compare isolation sources. Then, in one confirmed xoxF-free strain, grow with and without lanthanum and delete lanmodulin to see whether growth or metal uptake changes.
directions.title: What do lanmodulin-carrying bacteria without a confirmed xoxF use lanthanides for?
directions.why_it_matters: It would separate lanthanide handling from methanol oxidation and show a wider role for lanthanides in bacteria than the methylotroph picture suggests. If xoxF turns out to be present, lanmodulin simply tracks it.

directions.hypothesis: The lanmodulin gene tree disagrees with the species tree, and the gene sits next to mobile-element or insertion-like genes in some genomes, which points to horizontal transfer.
directions.outcomes: Support: clear gene-tree/species-tree conflict, copies in mobile-associated contexts, and base composition unlike the host. Refutation: the gene tree follows the species tree and the neighbourhood is conserved, which means vertical inheritance with lineage-specific loss.
directions.prior_work: PMID 30351021, 35814700 and 37259003 characterise single lanmodulins; none reconstructs how the gene moved among lineages.
directions.question: Lanmodulin occurs only in three alpha-Proteobacterial methylotroph families. Was it inherited from a common ancestor and lost elsewhere, or passed sideways between lineages that share habitats?
directions.readiness_basis: Genome and annotation data are present; tree building and synteny comparison need new computation.
directions.test: Using the Pangenome Collection, build a gene tree for lanmodulin proteins from the bakta-validated genomes and compare it with the species tree. Test whether closely related species differ in carrying lanmodulin. Check the flanking genes of each copy for transposases, integrases and phage genes, and compare the base composition of the gene with its host genome.
directions.title: Was lanmodulin spread by horizontal transfer among alpha-Proteobacterial methylotrophs?
directions.why_it_matters: It would explain the narrow distribution and show whether metal-handling proteins move between lineages in the same habitat, which bears on how lanthanide use evolves.

directions.hypothesis: A large share of xoxF carriers across phyla lack the downstream one-carbon pathways needed to use methanol, so the xoxF-over-mxaF excess reflects broad alcohol oxidation, not methylotrophy.
directions.outcomes: Support: many carriers lack the downstream route and the enzyme prefers longer alcohols. Refutation: nearly all carriers have a complete one-carbon route and the enzyme is most active on methanol.
directions.prior_work: PMID 29404411 and 26858104 show xoxF as the main methanol dehydrogenase in particular methylotrophs and PMID 41636527 reviews wider methylotrophic metabolism; this tests whether the genome-wide excess is methanol-related at all.
directions.question: If xoxF outnumbers mxaF so strongly, do most carriers actually run a full methanol-to-formaldehyde-to-energy route, or does xoxF mainly act on other alcohols or aldehydes in bacteria that are not methylotrophs?
directions.readiness_basis: The genome classification can be done on lakehouse data, but substrate preference requires enzyme assays.
directions.test: In the Pangenome Collection, classify xoxF-carrying genomes by presence of formaldehyde-oxidation and one-carbon assimilation genes, per phylum and with both annotation sources combined. Then, for non-methylotroph carriers in soil lineages such as Acidobacteriota, measure enzyme activity of purified XoxF against methanol, ethanol and other alcohols with and without lanthanides.
directions.title: Is xoxF mostly a methanol enzyme, or does it serve other alcohols in non-methylotrophs?
directions.why_it_matters: It would redefine the xoxF count as a measure of lanthanide-dependent alcohol chemistry, and change how xoxF abundance in soils and wetlands is read as methanol cycling.

directions.hypothesis: Lanthanide-dependent methylotrophs are enriched at lanthanide-rich sites of near-neutral pH but not in acidic, metal-laden drainage, where stress genes dominate.
directions.outcomes: Support: xoxF enrichment at neutral rare-earth-rich sites but not acidic ones, and lanthanum-stimulated enrichments only at neutral pH. Refutation: acidic sites are equally enriched, or neutral rare-earth sites show no excess over matched controls.
directions.prior_work: PMID 33848048 describes the microbiota of a river hit by rare-earth mining drainage, and PMID 38369453 finds lanthanide enzymes in weathered granite and soil; neither compares sites by acidity to see what gates lanthanide-dependent organisms.
directions.question: Acid-mine-drainage genomes from a rare-earth mining site carried little xoxF and no lanmodulin. Does acid and metal stress override lanthanide availability, so that xoxF enrichment appears only at rare-earth-rich sites with milder chemistry?
directions.readiness_basis: The earlier rare-earth set was small and from a single project, so more metagenomes or new enrichments are needed.
directions.test: Search NMDC Multi-omics and NMDC BioSamples for metagenomes from rare-earth-rich soils, weathered rock, mine tailings and acid drainage, plus matched non-rare-earth controls, and compare xoxF and lanmodulin carriage and stress-gene profiles by pH class. Then run methanol enrichments of neutral and acidic rare-earth-rich material with and without added lanthanum, and measure xoxF expression and lanthanide uptake.
directions.title: Do rare-earth-rich sites select lanthanide-dependent methylotrophs only when acidity does not dominate?
directions.why_it_matters: It would show that lanthanide supply alone does not recruit lanthanide-dependent organisms and that pH or co-occurring metals gate it. This sets where to look for them in rare-earth mining and recovery settings.

directions.hypothesis: Acid-drainage genomes from rare-earth sites carry lanthanide-binding proteins with calcium-binding-like motifs but no match to known families, and these bind lanthanides more strongly than calcium.
directions.outcomes: Support: candidates enriched at the rare-earth site over the control that bind lanthanides preferentially. Refutation: candidates are equally common in the control or bind calcium as well as lanthanides.
directions.prior_work: PMID 34432449 and 37259003 characterise lanmodulin binding; this searches for binders that annotation-based detection could not find.
